title: Make LLM Inference Affordable to Everyone: Augmenting GPU Memory with NDP-DIMM
problem: Deploying large LLMs (e.g., LLaMA2-70B) on consumer-grade GPUs with limited VRAM is impractical; offloading model weights to host DRAM or NVMe storage creates severe bandwidth bottlenecks on the PCIe interconnect, resulting in very low inference throughput.
method: Hermes partitions LLM weights into 'hot' neurons (~20% of parameters, ~80% of compute) and 'cold' neurons (~80% of parameters, ~20% of compute) based on activation sparsity. Hot neurons are mapped to the consumer GPU for compute-efficient execution, while cold neurons are offloaded to near-data processing (NDP) units embedded in commodity DRAM DIMMs. A lightweight runtime predictor dynamically classifies neurons as hot or cold based on input activations. A window-based online scheduler maintains load balance across multiple NDP-DIMM modules, enabling pipelined heterogeneous execution between GPU and NDP-DIMMs.

title: ARTERY: Fast Quantum Feedback using Branch Prediction
problem: Quantum feedback in dynamic circuits introduces significant latency because each feedback branch must wait for measurement results to propagate through classical decoding and control, blocking gate execution and degrading circuit fidelity. The dynamic nature of mid-circuit measurement prevents speculative execution under current quantum control hardware.
method: ARTERY applies branch prediction to quantum feedback by combining two sources of information: historical statistics of branch outcomes and a real-time readout-pulse trajectory predictor that analyzes the in-flight pulse shape to predict the qubit state before full demodulation is complete. A reconciled branch predictor fuses these two signals to allow downstream gates to begin executing speculatively. Hardware support includes a scalable inter-FPGA backplane for feedback routing, a trigger mechanism for dynamic instruction timing, and an adaptive pulse sampling technique to maximize bandwidth.

title: Tally: Non-Intrusive Performance Isolation for Concurrent Deep Learning Workloads
problem: GPU sharing for concurrent deep learning workloads suffers from high interference between co-running jobs, causing up to 188.9% latency overhead on high-priority inference tasks. Existing GPU sharing mechanisms impose high integration costs, offer inadequate performance isolation, and have limited application compatibility.
method: Tally implements a non-intrusive GPU sharing mechanism based on fine-grained thread-block-level kernel scheduling. It intercepts GPU kernel launches and dynamically schedules thread blocks across co-running workloads without requiring application modification, allowing the system to control interference between high-priority inference and best-effort training tasks at the thread-block granularity rather than at the kernel or process level.

title: HardHarvest: Hardware-Supported Core Harvesting for Microservices
problem: Software core harvesting—where batch 'Harvest VMs' temporarily steal idle cores from latency-critical 'Primary VMs'—incurs prohibitive overheads (hypervisor calls, TLB/cache flushes, context switches) that are acceptable for monolithic applications but intolerable for sub-millisecond microservices.
method: HardHarvest implements core harvesting entirely in hardware by adding in-hardware request scheduling logic that detects idle cores in Primary VMs and assigns them to Harvest VM tasks without hypervisor intervention. TLBs and caches are partitioned between Primary and Harvest VMs using a smart replacement algorithm that protects Primary VM working sets, enabling rapid context transfer without full TLB/cache flushes. The hardware scheduler monitors Primary VM request queues and preempts Harvest VM work before Primary VM tail latency is impacted.

title: PIMnet: A Domain-Specific Network for Efficient Collective Communication in Scalable PIM
problem: PIM compute units can only access their local memory; inter-bank communication in PIM systems must route through the host CPU, which becomes a bottleneck for collective communication operations (e.g., all-reduce, broadcast) that are common in many workloads, limiting PIM's scalability.
method: PIMnet is a PIM-controlled interconnection network providing direct connectivity between PIM compute units across banks and chips, bypassing the host CPU. It exploits bandwidth parallelism by allowing concurrent inter-bank and inter-chip communication. The network topology matches the DRAM packaging hierarchy with a multi-tier architecture (intra-chip and inter-chip tiers). Unlike traditional network-on-chip designs, PIMnet is managed by the PIM logic itself, not the host, to minimize hardware overhead and optimize collective communication patterns.

title: MoC-System: Efficient Fault Tolerance for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Model Training
problem: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs have model parameter counts far exceeding dense models of equivalent compute cost, making checkpoint-based fault tolerance extremely expensive in terms of checkpoint size, write bandwidth, and recovery time for distributed training at >10k node scale.
method: MoC-System exploits the sparse activation pattern of MoE models: only a subset of experts is activated per token, so most expert parameters are not updated in any given training step. The system uses a Model-on-Checkpoint (MoC) approach that selectively checkpoints only the experts that were actually updated (activated) during a training step, avoiding checkpointing dormant expert parameters. This is combined with distributed checkpoint orchestration to overlap checkpoint I/O with forward/backward computation and expert-parallel sharding to minimize per-node checkpoint volume.

title: Symbiotic Task Scheduling and Data Prefetching
problem: Hardware task-parallel systems that operate with fine-grained tasks (approx. 100-cycle execution time) cannot benefit from conventional hardware prefetchers because tasks are too short for prefetches to complete before the task finishes, leaving DRAM latency fully exposed and undermining the performance gains of hardware task management.
method: The Task-Seeded Prefetcher (TSP) learns the data-access pattern of each task function type and issues prefetches as soon as a task descriptor is queued by the hardware task scheduler, using the descriptor as a seed to identify which memory addresses the task will access. The Memory Response Task Scheduler (MRS) augments the baseline task-to-core dispatch policy by monitoring prefetch completion status from TSP: when a task's prefetches are done, MRS preferentially dispatches it to a ready core, maximizing prefetch utilization without stalling the pipeline. Together, TSP and MRS form a symbiotic pair where scheduling drives prefetching and prefetch status informs scheduling.

title: FLEXPROF: Flexible, Side-Channel-Free Memory Access
problem: Secure memory controllers that prevent microarchitectural side-channels by allocating fixed 'turns' to co-scheduled VMs impose a ~2x performance slowdown because the schedule must conservatively handle worst-case mixed read/write patterns, leaving memory bus utilization inefficient.
method: FlexProf introduces two types of memory controller turns: read-optimized turns and write-optimized turns, selected via coarse-grain application profiling that observes the read/write ratio without leaking sensitive information. Each turn type is sized and structured for its dominant operation. Flexibility is added so that a read-optimized turn can opportunistically issue writes when read slots are idle (and vice versa), improving utilization while preserving the fixed-turn structure needed to prevent timing side-channels between VMs.

title: Hierarchical Prefetching: A Software-Hardware Instruction Prefetcher for Server Applications
problem: Server-side applications have large instruction working sets that cause severe front-end bottlenecks even with state-of-the-art fetch-directed instruction prefetching (FDIP), because record-and-replay prefetchers lose coverage and timeliness when actual control flow diverges from predicted control flow.
method: Hierarchical Prefetching identifies coarse-grained functionality blocks called Bundles—spanning tens to hundreds of kilobytes of code—through lightweight static software analysis of the server binary. Hardware then uses a compact record-and-replay mechanism (under 2KB of on-chip SRAM) that prefetches entire Bundles when a bundle entry point is detected, rather than individual cache lines. Most Bundle metadata is stored in main memory, keeping on-chip storage minimal. The bundle formation analysis groups functionally related code regions that tend to execute together, tolerating control flow variability by prefetching the entire functional region rather than a precise sequence.

title: DejaVuzz: Disclosing Transient Execution Bugs with Dynamic Swappable Memory and Differential Information Flow Tracking Assisted Processor Fuzzing
problem: Existing hardware fuzzers for detecting transient execution vulnerabilities (e.g., Spectre, Meltdown variants) suffer from poor microarchitectural controllability and observability: they cannot reliably set up the precise microarchitectural state needed to trigger transient execution paths, nor detect covert information leakage resulting from such paths.
method: DejaVuzz introduces two synergistic mechanisms: Dynamic Swappable Memory (DSM), which swaps physical memory pages at runtime to precisely control the microarchitectural state of TLBs, caches, and branch predictors needed to trigger transient execution; and Differential Information Flow Tracking (DIFT), which instruments the processor simulator to observe whether secret data leaks through transient microarchitectural side channels. The fuzzer generates test programs that exercise transient execution windows by leveraging DSM to reset microarchitectural state between tests, and uses DIFT differential analysis to detect when information from a secret source reaches an observable side channel (e.g., cache timing). This enables both high coverage and precise detection of leakage.

title: HATT: Hamiltonian Adaptive Ternary Tree for Optimizing Fermion-to-Qubit Mapping
problem: Mapping Fermionic quantum systems to qubit systems produces Hamiltonians with high Pauli weight, inflating quantum circuit gate count and depth. Existing Fermion-to-qubit mappings are not tailored to specific Hamiltonian structures, leading to unnecessary overhead.
method: HATT constructs ternary tree-based Fermion-to-qubit mappings using a bottom-up procedure that is adaptive to the specific Fermionic Hamiltonian being compiled. The algorithm analyzes Hamiltonian term structure to guide tree construction, reducing Pauli weight compared to generic mappings such as Jordan-Wigner or Bravyi-Kitaev. The complexity is reduced from O(N^4) to O(N^3) while preserving vacuum state properties required for correctness of simulation.

title: Palermo: Improving the Performance of Oblivious Memory using Protocol-Hardware Co-Design
problem: Oblivious RAM (ORAM) protocols impose severe performance penalties because classical ORAM enforces strict sequential dependencies between memory operations, leaving memory bandwidth severely underutilized. Prior prefetching and request-elimination approaches are fragile under low-locality workloads and create additional ORAM stash pressure overhead.
method: Palermo redesigns the RingORAM protocol to allow overlapping of memory operations both within a single ORAM request and across multiple concurrent requests, without violating correctness or security invariants. A dedicated ORAM controller hardware implements this relaxed protocol by concurrently issuing memory requests while tracking and enforcing only the necessary inter-request dependencies to maintain a consistent ORAM tree view. The architecture manages stash and position-map structures in hardware to prevent stash overflow while enabling pipelined DRAM accesses.

title: Cooperative Graceful Degradation in Containerized Clouds
problem: Cloud operators lack a mechanism to automatically perform graceful degradation of applications during failures or capacity crunch while simultaneously satisfying application availability requirements and operator infrastructure objectives.
method: Phoenix uses criticality tags on containers to distinguish critical from non-critical services, then applies diagonal scaling—turning off non-critical containers during capacity crunch to free resources for critical services. A Kubernetes-atop controller implements this cooperative graceful degradation by jointly optimizing for both application-defined criticality constraints and operator-level infrastructure objectives. Phoenix handles failures in a cluster of 100,000 nodes within 10 seconds.

title: Reinforcement Learning-Guided Graph State Generation in Photonic Quantum Computers
problem: In photonic quantum computers (PQCs), generating graph states (entangled photon collections) requires finding an optimal generation sequence over quantum emitters, where three fidelity-critical metrics — generation time, number of emitters used, and number of CZ gates — are jointly minimized. Existing compilation frameworks either face exponential search complexity or fail to guarantee optimal results due to their non-deterministic properties.
method: RLGS (Reinforcement Learning-guided Graph State generation) frames the generation sequence problem as an RL optimization task. A map-based abstraction extracts and aligns two-qubit gate dependencies from quantum circuits into a structured representation, enabling the RL agent to detect dependency patterns and search for generation sequences that simultaneously reduce generation time, emitter count, and CZ gate insertions. The framework balances gate serialization depth against crosstalk reduction.

title: From Optimal to Practical: Efficient Micro-op Cache Replacement Policies for Data Center Applications
problem: Data center applications suffer frequent micro-op (uop) cache misses because no effective uop-cache-specific replacement policy exists; the uop cache has fundamentally different cost characteristics from conventional caches (variable and disproportional miss costs, partial hits), making standard policies like LRU and even Belady's algorithm suboptimal.
method: FLACK is introduced as a near-optimal offline replacement policy that accounts for uop cache-specific properties: variable miss costs (due to disproportional re-fetch penalties) and partial hits (when only some micro-ops of an instruction group are cached). FLACK substantially outperforms Belady's algorithm, establishing a new uop-cache-specific optimality bound. FURBYS is then designed as a practical online policy that mimics FLACK via profile-guided methods, using three components: (1) whole-execution hit/miss profiles per static instruction, (2) detection of locally/transiently hot data, and (3) selective ignorance of entries with profiled low hit rates during replacement decisions.

title: Systematic CXL Memory Characterization and Performance Analysis at Scale
problem: CXL-attached memory introduces sub-microsecond latency overheads (140-410 ns) relative to local DRAM, but the performance impact across diverse devices, CPU platforms, and workloads is poorly understood, including tail latencies, prefetcher behavior, and bottleneck localization.
method: Melody is a characterization framework that runs 265 workloads across 4 real CXL devices, 5 CPU platforms, and 7 injected latency levels to comprehensively profile CXL memory performance. It introduces SPA (Sub-operation Performance Analysis), a novel methodology that decomposes memory access latency into sub-operations to pinpoint CXL-specific bottlenecks. Melody also measures and discloses CXL tail latency distributions for the first time, and characterizes CPU hardware prefetcher effectiveness (and failures) under CXL latency conditions.
